name: Erik Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We are not linked to employers, unions, government or AI companies, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Erik Moreau, 43, and a junior lineworker for an electricity company. The vocational certificate got me in, but I’m still learning how to spot a fault from the ground before the senior worker sends us up. Yesterday we replaced a cracked insulator after the street had lost power; I carried tools, checked the exclusion zone and watched the lift. I like seeing a repair done properly, even if it takes longer than the dispatch sheet said.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the job sit with the rest of your life?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Amira handles the school run for our two children when I start early, and I take the evening shift when she has a late day at her clinic. The mortgage is steady and we have more than six months of expenses saved. I earn toward the high end because I take callouts, and there are plenty of utilities nearby, though I would rather earn competence here first. I use an AI tool now and then to sort my notes, usually after somebody else has tried a feature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues the office can have its quicker forms if our repair instructions still make sense. A modest time saving is welcome at the end of a long shift. I would not call a cleaner spreadsheet a new way to fix a cable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be comfortable with this because I still need years on the tools. Being junior at 43 is awkward enough without the method changing every week. Our savings and my callout pay make the household fairly secure, but I want to become useful enough that the crew asks for me by name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep taking supervised callouts, and on Fridays I’d compare my paper fault notes with the work order record. If the office offers an AI draft of the report, I’d try it only after a coworker shows me the checks. In the first year I’d keep my current shifts and correct any wrong asset number before I sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I know how to fit this into a working day, and I don’t feel my pay is at risk. The only thing I dislike is a sloppy record following us to the next job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you remember a record you had to correct?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a report listed the wrong pole number; I caught it because I’d copied the plate into my pocket book. The next crew would have lost an hour looking in the wrong place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the household do anything differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amira and I would leave our mortgage plan alone. We might enjoy an evening without me retyping a form, but that is not a reason to change the children’s plans.

say: I would welcome **quicker forms** if field instructions remain clear.
I would remind colleagues that a cleaner **spreadsheet** does not repair a cable.
think: I need more **time on tools** before I feel settled as a lineworker.
Our **savings and callout pay** make the household secure in this mild picture.
do: Keep taking **supervised callouts** and compare Friday notes with work orders.
Try the **AI report draft** after a coworker explains its checks, then correct asset numbers.
feel: Calm about my income, but bothered by **sloppy records** that reach the next crew.
S0.quote: I would not call a cleaner spreadsheet a new way to fix a cable.
fieldNote: Erik’s example of the **wrong pole number** makes his interest in faster reports conditional on traceable field checks.
He is a **steady adopter** who waits for a coworker’s demonstration, while strong savings support his calm outlook.

steps.text: Keep taking supervised repair callouts on current shifts
Try the AI report draft after a coworker demonstrates its checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the booking and buying people will see the first big changes, while we still have physical repairs to do. I’d like the new dispatch route to be tested on a rainy shift before anyone sets a quota from it. If it works, I’ll use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry that quicker planning means fewer people to answer when a part is missing. Our crew might lose hours waiting and then be blamed for a slow repair. I might lose some callout pay if the schedule gets tighter, but regular pay and the reserve would still carry the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the experienced crew to show me the new dispatch screen on a quiet day, then compare its route to actual travel for a month. I’d note missing stock on each ticket and bring the list to the supervisor. In the first year I’d keep taking repair shifts and ask for a corrected quota if our times are consistently wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because the work is still there but the day might be measured badly. I’m willing to learn a tool that helps. I am not eager to argue with a dashboard when a cable is lying across the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would you bring about missing parts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d write the part number and the time we waited for a replacement, so the supervisor can see where the delay came from. A complaint with no detail gets lost by Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household purchase would move first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If callouts fell for two months, Amira and I would postpone replacing the living-room sofa. I would not touch the emergency account for furniture while a new rota is settling.

say: I would welcome **tested dispatch** while asking for rainy-shift evidence before setting quotas.
I would point out that **parts delays** still need a person to resolve them.
think: Fewer **buying staff** could leave crews waiting for parts and blamed for slow repairs.
Some **callout pay** might go, although regular pay and savings cover our mortgage.
do: Learn the **dispatch screen** from experienced coworkers and compare routes for a month.
Log **missing parts** on tickets and seek a corrected quota from the supervisor.
Continue paid **repair shifts** through the first year.
feel: Uneasy about **bad measurements**, while open to a useful proven tool.
S1.quote: I am not eager to argue with a dashboard when a cable is lying across the road.
fieldNote: Erik’s concern is an **unfair quota** caused by lost buying staff, rather than immediate disappearance of physical repair work.
His plan combines a **coworker demonstration** with a month of route and stock evidence before asking for changes.

steps.text: Learn the dispatch screen and compare routes for one month
Continue paid repair shifts under the new rota
Postpone the living-room sofa if callout pay falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that thinking AI in 2028 could clear the office, but it does not climb for us until capable robots come around 2031. The company should be honest about that three-year gap. I’d ask for the names of posts it expects to keep, not a promise that everyone will supervise a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 45 I’d expect to keep earning on the line while the office changes. At 48 the repair robots might remove half the crew work, or none of it for a while; I honestly cannot tell. I’m junior, so a cut roster could reach me first. The reserve buys search time, and nearby utilities help, but the children and mortgage still depend on a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask the training office whether its network inspection course has funded places and actual vacancies. I’d keep taking paid callouts through 2028 and 2029 and ask to shadow a field inspector for two shifts if allowed. In 2031, if robots cut our rota, I’d apply for inspection and repair vacancies at the nearby utilities and postpone our summer trip until the new income is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can make a plan, but I can’t put a guarantee on a vacancy. There is something cruel about losing the climb just when I finally stop needing directions at every pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would shadowing teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the inspector what a full week looks like, including paperwork and weather calls. A two-day visit could tell me whether I want that work before I ask the family to rely on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Amira about the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Amira the household is not in immediate danger, because of the reserve. I would also tell her that we need to review the budget if my shift letter changes in 2031.

say: I would mark **2028 office change** separately from repair robots arriving around 2031.
I would ask for **named retained posts** instead of a broad promise of supervision jobs.
think: I expect **paid linework** during the three-year gap, but my junior position could face a cut after 2031.
Our **reserve** and local utilities help, yet a wage still pays for our children and mortgage.
do: Ask about **funded inspection training** and shadow an inspector if allowed.
Apply to nearby **utilities** and postpone summer travel if robots cut shifts in 2031.
feel: Anxious about a **cut roster**, though I can still seek training and local work.
S2.quote: There is something cruel about losing the climb just when I finally stop needing directions at every pole.
fieldNote: He expects continued **physical work after 2028** and names 2031 as the uncertain point for his own crew.
He tests a possible **inspection route** through funded training and job shadowing before relying on that income.

steps.text: Request funded inspection training if places and jobs exist
Apply to nearby utilities if crews shrink in 2031
Postpone the summer trip if field income drops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company for a trial that ordinary repair crews can watch and question. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and the hands-on robots around 2034, so we have time to test the safety claims. I’d tell the yard to watch the actual crew. A filmed demo is not the same as a repair at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be 48 when the thinking work changes and 51 when the robots arrive. That gives me years to become competent and perhaps move toward inspection, though I cannot bank on that job. The children will be older, and our mortgage should be lower, but neither fact pays the bills without income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d complete my supervised fault list and ask a senior worker to check it. If the inspection course gets funded, I’d enroll after asking what vacancies it feeds. In 2032 I’d apply for an internal inspection opening and keep working on the repair truck; in 2034 I’d compare outside utility offers if our line shifts drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more settled than in the two-year picture. I can see a sequence of small choices. I’d still feel nervous if management showed a robot and stopped talking about the people assigned to watch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at a field trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask whether the robot can tell old paint from a heat mark on a fitting. If it cannot, a person needs to examine the part before it signs off a repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge an inspection offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the daytime inspection wage against my callout wage with Amira. A safer schedule would be good for family life, but we cannot just ignore the amount coming in.

say: I would ask for **night repair trials** before accepting robot safety claims.
I would keep the **2031 and 2034** changes separate when talking with crews.
think: I can gain **field competence** before robots arrive, though an inspection post is uncertain.
Our older children and smaller **mortgage balance** do not remove our need for income.
do: Complete my **supervised fault list** and have a senior worker review it.
Enroll in **funded inspection training** if it leads to vacancies.
Apply for an **inspection opening** in 2032 while continuing paid repairs.
feel: Uneasy, with enough **time for choices** and a clear concern about machine sign-off.
S3.quote: A filmed demo is not the same as a repair at night.
fieldNote: His longer horizon supports a **stepwise skill plan** grounded in supervised faults, course funding and a posted vacancy.
He evaluates inspection against **actual callout pay**, even though a daytime schedule would help family life.

steps.text: Keep repairing lines and complete the supervised fault list
Enroll in funded inspection training if vacancies follow
Apply for an internal inspection opening in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew we have a decade to collect facts. Thinking AI comes in 2036 and repair robots around 2039; each year the company should tell us which tasks and posts have changed. I’d rather see the roster than a prediction chart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be 53 at the first date and 56 at the second. Our children would be grown, so I’m not budgeting for school lunches forever, and I might want fewer night calls. Still, I have no retirement figure in my hand and I cannot assume a pension covers the mortgage. If there are safe daytime posts, I’d like to see whether one fits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask payroll for a retirement estimate and put it next to the mortgage repayment schedule with Amira. I’d keep earning on the line while building enough experience to apply for an inspection role. In 2037 I’d apply if a daytime post is advertised at workable pay; in 2039 I’d decide about fewer nights only after seeing the actual household income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years. The long warning gives me space to get good at this job and check the numbers. I might be uneasy later if the annual roster shows a fast drop, but that is not where I am today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which retirement number matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want the retirement estimate per month, after deductions, rather than a headline total. We have savings, but I don’t want to mistake a cash cushion for a regular wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children be part of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amira and I could talk to our grown children about plans by then, but I would not expect them to fund us. The inspection application would be mine to make, not theirs.

say: I would ask for a yearly **post count** through 2039.
I would distinguish the **2036 thinking shift** from later field robots.
think: Our children will be **grown**, and I might prefer fewer night calls at 56.
I cannot assume **retirement income** pays the mortgage without a real estimate.
do: Request a **monthly retirement estimate** and compare it with the mortgage now.
Continue paid **linework** while building inspection experience.
Apply for a **daytime inspection post** in 2037 if the wage works.
feel: Calm about the next few years, with a future **roster decline** worth watching.
S4.quote: I’d rather see the roster than a prediction chart.
fieldNote: Erik avoids treating 56 as an automatic **retirement date**, asking for a monthly figure before cutting night work.
His preparation involves **continued paid repairs** and a conditional daytime application, while grown children are not treated as earners.

steps.text: Continue paid linework and build inspection experience
Apply for a daytime inspection post in 2037 if viable

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I can get used to a new tool, but I cannot pack years of field judgment into two winters. Paid inspection training tied to a real vacancy would help, along with clear dates for which crew tasks might change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who corrects the machine’s record when the pole number is wrong? A wrong record can send the next crew to the wrong street. I want a simple way for the person on site to fix it before anyone acts on it.

headlineQuote: A wrong record can send the next crew to the wrong street.
portrait: Erik is a **43-year-old junior lineworker** with vocational training, strong savings, high callout pay, two school-age children and a mortgage.
He uses AI **now and then** for notes, usually after coworkers demonstrate a feature, and checks records against field details.
He expects **desk work** to change before line repairs and considers his junior crew place vulnerable once capable robots arrive.
Across scenarios he keeps **paid repairs** going while testing dispatch, seeking funded inspection training and checking actual vacancies.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because he cannot gain several years of line judgment before fast staffing decisions.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid inspection training** linked to a vacancy and a clear timetable for changes to crew work.
